title: Sample mean
parts: The arithmetic mean of observations in a sample.
note: A bar over x means a sample mean. μ usually denotes a population mean.

title: Standard deviation
parts: The population standard deviation, the square root of its variance.
example: For a population consisting of 0 and 4, the mean is 2, the variance is 4 and σ=2.
note: Lowercase σ often denotes spread. Uppercase Σ or ∑ marks summation.
wrong: The population variance before taking the square root.

title: Sample proportion
parts: The observed fraction of the sample in the category of interest.
example: If 18 out of 60 students walk to school, p̂=18/60=0.3.
note: The hat marks a sample estimate. The population proportion may differ.
wrong: The exact proportion of the whole population.

title: Standard score
parts: The number of population standard deviations that x is above or below μ.
example: With μ=70, σ=10 and x=50, z=−2.
note: A negative z-score places a value below the mean.
wrong: The distance from the mean in the original units.

title: Confidence interval
parts: An approximate 95% confidence interval from the estimate minus the margin to the estimate plus it.
example: If p̂=0.50 and SE=0.02, the interval is about [0.461,0.539].
note: Under the method’s assumptions, about 95% of such intervals cover the fixed true value in repeated sampling.
wrong: 95% of the observations lie inside the interval.

title: Null hypothesis
parts: The null hypothesis claims the population proportion equals p₀.
example: To test a claim of 50% support, write H₀:p=0.50 and compare a sample against that claim.
note: The claim is about the population, rather than the exact result of a sample.
wrong: The sample proportion must be exactly p₀.

title: p-value
parts: Under the null, the probability of a test result at least as extreme as the one observed in the direction or directions tested.
example: For a fair coin, the chance of all ten tosses landing on the same side is 2×(½)¹⁰ ≈ 0.002. That is the two-sided p-value for 10 heads.
note: This probability is computed assuming the null.
wrong: The probability that the null hypothesis is true.

title: Pearson correlation
parts: The sample Pearson correlation coefficient, between −1 and 1.
example: For x values 1,2,3 paired with y values 3,2,1, r=−1.
note: Correlation measures linear association. It does not establish causation.
wrong: The slope of the line through the data in original units.

title: Standard error of the sample mean
parts: The standard deviation of the sample mean for n independent observations with population standard deviation σ.
example: If σ=12 and n=36, the standard error is 2.
note: Standard error describes how a statistic varies from sample to sample.
wrong: The standard deviation of each individual observation is σ/√n.
